theory.contentHtml:
You manage data for a retail chain: dozens of revenue tables arrive every day, and the same calculations - discounts, daily summaries, metric comparisons - repeat everywhere. Writing flexible functions is the only way to stop copy-pasting formulas, and it also lays the foundation for the apply family in the next lesson.

📑 Lesson contents:

  • 1. Default parameters
  • 2. Returning multiple values with a list
  • 3. Anonymous functions
  • 4. Passing functions as arguments
  • Key takeaways

1. Default parameters

Your retail chain runs a member discount program: most products get 10% off, and only occasionally is there a deeper sale. Instead of forcing every caller to remember to pass the discount rate, you set a default value right in the function definition with the syntax parameter = value:

apply_discount <- function(price, rate = 0.1) {
  round(price * (1 - rate), 2)
}

apply_discount(200000)
apply_discount(200000, rate = 0.25)

Output:

[1] 180000
[1] 150000

The first call doesn't pass rate, so R uses 0.1. The second call passes rate = 0.25 to override it. When a function has several parameters, calling with names (rate = 0.25) makes the code easier to read and independent of parameter order.

2. Returning multiple values with a list

A function in R returns only one object - the value of the last expression (or whatever you put in return()). To return several numbers at once - total revenue, the biggest order, the number of orders that day - wrap them all in a named list:

summarize_day <- function(revenue_vec) {
  list(
    total = sum(revenue_vec),
    best = max(revenue_vec),
    n_orders = length(revenue_vec)
  )
}

report <- summarize_day(c(120, 300, 250, 180))
report$total
report$best
report$n_orders

Output:

[1] 850
[1] 300
[1] 4

Whoever receives the result accesses each component with $ (or [[ ]]). This pattern shows up all over R itself: lm(), t.test()... all return named lists like this.

3. Anonymous functions

Not every function deserves a name. For a small transformation used only once, R lets you write an anonymous function - a function with no name. Since R 4.1 there is also the shorthand syntax \(x), fully equivalent to function(x):

add_vat <- function(x) x * 1.1
add_vat_short <- \(x) x * 1.1

add_vat(500)
add_vat_short(500)

Output:

[1] 550
[1] 550

Here we still assign the functions to variables so the two styles are easy to compare. The real power of anonymous functions is using them right in place, with no assignment - you'll see them go hand in hand with the apply family in the next lesson.

4. Passing functions as arguments

In R, functions are first-class objects: just like a vector or a data.frame, a function can be assigned to a variable and passed into another function. That lets you write one shared skeleton function while the caller decides the specific calculation:

report_metric <- function(revenue_vec, metric_fn) {
  metric_fn(revenue_vec)
}

daily_revenue <- c(500, 700, 650, 900)
report_metric(daily_revenue, mean)
report_metric(daily_revenue, max)
report_metric(daily_revenue, \(x) sum(x > 600))

Output:

[1] 687.5
[1] 900
[1] 3

The same report_metric, three different questions: the daily average, the best day, and how many days beat the 600 mark - the last one uses an anonymous function written inline. Note: pass mean (the bare function name, no parentheses), because adding parentheses means calling the function immediately:

# Wrong - mean() runs immediately with no data instead of being passed along
report_metric(daily_revenue, mean())

Key takeaways

  • When passing a function as an argument, use the bare name (mean), not parentheses (mean()).
  • The \(x) syntax only exists from R 4.1 onward; function(x) works on every version.
  • A function returns only the value of its last expression - the intermediate lines don't "leak" out on their own; to return several values, wrap them in a named list.
  • Pull elements out of a list with report$total or report[["total"]]; using report["total"] (single brackets) gives you back a sub-list, not the value inside.
  • Default parameters are for the value "used 90% of the time"; don't overuse them to the point where readers can't tell what the function actually needs.

theory.contentHtml:
Thirty days of revenue, eight stores, and a familiar question from your boss: "what's the average per store?". You could write a ten-line for loop - or let the apply family answer it in one line.

📑 Lesson contents:

  • 1. Why the apply family
  • 2. lapply returns a list
  • 3. sapply simplifies the result
  • 4. tapply groups by factor
  • Key takeaways

1. Why the apply family

The "classic" way to apply a calculation to every element is a for loop: initialize a container, loop over the indices, assign each result:

daily_revenue <- c(1200, 950, 1480)
with_vat <- numeric(length(daily_revenue))
for (i in seq_along(daily_revenue)) {
  with_vat[i] <- daily_revenue[i] * 1.1
}
with_vat

Output:

[1] 1320 1045 1628

Four lines just to "multiply each element by 1.1". (This particular operation can be vectorized - daily_revenue * 1.1 does it - but plenty of operations have no ready-made vectorized form, for example computing the mean of EACH store in a list.) The apply family exists to manage both the loop and the result container for you: you only declare "which data" and "which function".

2. lapply returns a list

lapply(X, FUN) applies the function FUN to every element of X and returns a list of the same length:

store_revenue <- list(
  Hanoi = c(500, 700),
  Danang = c(300, 400, 350)
)
lapply(store_revenue, mean)

Output:

$Hanoi
[1] 600

$Danang
[1] 350

Each input element (one store's revenue vector) yields exactly one output element. lapply ALWAYS returns a list - even when every result is just a single number, as above.

3. sapply simplifies the result

sapply is exactly lapply plus a "simplify" step: if every result is a single value, it collapses them all into a named vector - far more compact to read and compute with:

store_revenue <- list(
  Hanoi = c(500, 700),
  Danang = c(300, 400, 350)
)
sapply(store_revenue, mean)

Output:

 Hanoi Danang
   600    350

sapply pairs very naturally with the anonymous functions from the previous lesson - for example, labeling each day against a revenue threshold:

daily_revenue <- c(520, 480, 610, 700)
sapply(daily_revenue, \(x) if (x >= 600) "high" else "low")

Output:

[1] "low"  "low"  "high" "high"

(This example just illustrates the pattern; for a simple comparison like this, vectorized ifelse is still cleaner. sapply shines when the applied function is complex and multi-step.)

4. tapply groups by factor

Real-world data rarely comes pre-split into a list per store - it's usually two parallel columns: store name and revenue. With a for loop, you would have to find the unique store list yourself, filter each group yourself, and collect the results yourself. tapply(values, groups, FUN) does all three in a single call - it groups values by the labels in groups and applies FUN to each group:

store <- c("Hanoi", "Danang", "Hanoi", "Danang", "Hanoi")
revenue <- c(500, 300, 700, 400, 600)
tapply(revenue, store, mean)

Output:

Danang  Hanoi
   350    600

store is a character vector - tapply converts it to a factor automatically, and the groups are ordered A→Z by label, not by order of appearance in the data. Combine it with an anonymous function to ask a harder question - each store's revenue range:

store <- c("Hanoi", "Danang", "Hanoi", "Danang")
revenue <- c(500, 300, 700, 400)
tapply(revenue, store, \(x) max(x) - min(x))

Output:

Danang  Hanoi
   100    200

Key takeaways

  • lapply ALWAYS returns a list; sapply can only simplify when every result has length 1 - otherwise it silently returns a list just like lapply, which can surprise you in the next calculation step.
  • tapply results are ordered by the sorted group labels (A→Z), not by order of appearance in the data.
  • The two vectors passed to tapply must have the same length - a mismatch errors out immediately.
  • Pass the bare function name (mean), don't call the function (mean()).
  • If an operation can be vectorized (x * 1.1), just vectorize it directly - faster and cleaner than both for loops and apply.

questions.prompt: The function set_price <- function(base, margin = 0.2) base * (1 + margin) is called as set_price(100). What does it return?

options.label: A
options.text: An error because the margin argument is missing

questions.explanation: margin has a default value of 0.2, so it doesn't have to be passed. The result is 100 * (1 + 0.2) = 120. You only override it when you want a different rate, e.g. set_price(100, margin = 0.5).

questions.prompt: A function needs to return both the total revenue and the number of orders at the same time. What is the standard way in R?

options.label: A
options.text: Call return() twice, once per value

options.label: B
options.text: Wrap both in a named list and return it, e.g. list(total = ..., n_orders = ...)

options.label: C
options.text: Write the second value into a global variable

options.label: D
options.text: R doesn't support this - you must split it into two functions

questions.explanation: An R function returns only a single object; the second return() is never reached. Wrapping multiple values in a named list is the standard pattern; the caller accesses them with $total, $n_orders.

questions.prompt: In R 4.1 and later, which of these is equivalent to \(x) x * 2?

options.label: A
options.text: function(x) x * 2

options.label: B
options.text: function(x = 2) x

options.label: D
options.text: None - \(x) is the required syntax for anonymous functions

questions.explanation: \(x) is just a shorthand for function(x), added in R 4.1 - the two are fully equivalent. The => syntax belongs to JavaScript and doesn't exist in R.

questions.prompt: store_revenue is a list of 3 revenue vectors for 3 stores. What does lapply(store_revenue, mean) return?

options.label: A
options.text: A numeric vector with 3 elements

options.label: B
options.text: A list of 3 elements, each one being the mean of one store

options.label: C
options.text: A data.frame with 3 rows

options.label: D
options.text: A single number - the mean of the whole chain

questions.explanation: lapply ALWAYS returns a list of the same length as its input, even when each result is just a single number. Use sapply if you want a named vector.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between sapply and lapply when applying the same function to the same list?

options.label: A
options.text: sapply always runs many times faster

options.label: B
options.text: sapply tries to simplify the result into a vector, while lapply always keeps it as a list

options.label: C
options.text: lapply only accepts built-in functions, not anonymous functions

options.label: D
options.text: sapply can only be applied to a data.frame

questions.explanation: sapply = lapply + a simplify step: when every result is a single value, it collapses them into a named vector. When it can't simplify, sapply returns a list exactly like lapply. Both accept anonymous functions just fine.

questions.prompt: You have two vectors of the same length: revenue (each day's revenue) and store (that day's store name). What does tapply(revenue, store, sum) do?

options.label: A
options.text: Computes the total of all of revenue and repeats that number for each store

options.label: B
options.text: Computes each store's total revenue separately, grouped by the values of store

options.label: C
options.text: Sorts revenue in A→Z order of store

options.label: D
options.text: Errors because store is a character vector, not a factor

questions.explanation: tapply groups the elements of revenue by the matching labels in store, then applies sum to each group. A character vector is converted to a factor automatically, and results are ordered by label A→Z.

practice.title: Average revenue per store
practice.summaryHtml: The retail chain's COO needs a quick ranking: which store is earning the most money on a per-day average? The data arrives as two parallel columns - store name and the revenue for each recorded day.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.html:
• Write a function avg_revenue_by_store(store_vec, revenue_vec) that takes two parallel vectors of the same length: store_vec is the store name, revenue_vec is the revenue for the corresponding day.
  • Compute each store's average daily revenue, rounded to 2 decimal places.
  • Return a data.frame with 2 columns: store - the store name, avg_revenue - the rounded average revenue.
  • Sort in descending order of avg_revenue; break ties by store from A to Z.
  • The row numbers of the returned data.frame restart from 1 (as in the examples).

sections.title: Example 1
sections.html:
Input: print(avg_revenue_by_store(c("Hanoi", "Danang", "Hanoi", "Danang", "Saigon"), c(500, 300, 700, 400, 450)))

Output:

   store avg_revenue
1  Hanoi         600
2 Saigon         450
3 Danang         350

sections.title: Example 2
sections.html:
Input: print(avg_revenue_by_store(c("Mall", "Airport", "Online", "Mall", "Airport"), c(100, 250, 333.333, 200, 50)))

Output:

    store avg_revenue
1  Online      333.33
2 Airport      150.00
3    Mall      150.00

chapters.title: DPLYR - A GRAMMAR OF DATA MANIPULATION

lessons.title: dplyr with filter, select, arrange and the pipe
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 5: dplyr with filter, select, arrange and the pipe

theory.contentHtml:
You manage data for a SaaS company: the subscriptions table has one row per paying customer, along with their plan and mrr - monthly recurring revenue. Questions like "which pro-plan customers are paying over $100 a month?" come up all the time - dplyr lets you answer them with lines of code that read like prose.

📑 Lesson contents:

  • 1. Why dplyr
  • 2. The pipe and the flow of data
  • 3. filter picks rows by condition
  • 4. select keeps the columns you need
  • 5. arrange sorts the result
  • Key takeaways

1. Why dplyr

Base R can filter and slice tables just fine. To see pro-plan customers along with what they pay, you would write:

subscriptions <- data.frame(
  customer = c("Skyline", "Nimbus", "Quartz", "Harbor"),
  plan = c("pro", "basic", "enterprise", "pro"),
  mrr = c(79, 29, 499, 79)
)
print(subscriptions[subscriptions$plan == "pro", c("customer", "mrr")])

Output:

  customer mrr
1  Skyline  79
4   Harbor  79

It works, but the table name has to be repeated twice, and as conditions grow more complex the command turns into a tangle of brackets that is hard to read. Notice the number column on the left: base R keeps the original row numbers (1 and 4) instead of renumbering.

dplyr - R's most popular data-manipulation package - is designed around one idea: each operation is a "verb" with a clear name like filter, select, arrange. Load it with:

library(dplyr)

The first time you call library(dplyr) in the sandbox, the system downloads the package, so it takes a few seconds - later calls are fast. On a desktop R, this command prints a few messages like "The following objects are masked" - informational notices, not errors. This course's sandbox strips them, so here the load shows no output at all; silence is normal.

2. The pipe and the flow of data

Before meeting the verbs, you need to get comfortable with the pipe operator |>. It takes the value on its left and passes it in as the first argument of the function on its right:

result <- data |>
  verb_one() |>
  verb_two()
# same as: result <- verb_two(verb_one(data))

Without the pipe, filtering then trimming columns then sorting means nesting functions inside-out, like arrange(select(filter(...))) - you have to read it from the inside out, which is exhausting. With the pipe, the steps line up in the order you think: take the table, filter, pick columns, sort.

3. filter picks rows by condition

filter keeps the rows that satisfy a condition:

library(dplyr)
subscriptions <- data.frame(
  customer = c("Skyline", "Nimbus", "Quartz", "Harbor"),
  plan = c("pro", "basic", "enterprise", "pro"),
  mrr = c(79, 29, 499, 79)
)
result <- subscriptions |> filter(plan == "pro")
print(result)

Output:

  customer plan mrr
1  Skyline  pro  79
2   Harbor  pro  79

Unlike base R in section 1, dplyr renumbers the rows starting from 1. Conditions use the familiar comparison operators (==, !=, >=, ...). Multiple conditions separated by commas are read as "AND":

library(dplyr)
subscriptions <- data.frame(
  customer = c("Skyline", "Nimbus", "Quartz", "Harbor", "Onyx"),
  plan = c("pro", "basic", "enterprise", "pro", "basic"),
  mrr = c(79, 29, 499, 129, 49)
)
result <- subscriptions |> filter(plan == "pro", mrr >= 100)
print(result)

Output:

  customer plan mrr
1   Harbor  pro 129

For "OR", use | instead of the comma.

4. select keeps the columns you need

filter trims rows, while select trims columns. A report for accounting only needs customer names and amounts:

library(dplyr)
subscriptions <- data.frame(
  customer = c("Skyline", "Nimbus", "Quartz"),
  plan = c("pro", "basic", "enterprise"),
  mrr = c(79, 29, 499)
)
result <- subscriptions |> select(customer, mrr)
print(result)

Output:

  customer mrr
1  Skyline  79
2   Nimbus  29
3   Quartz 499

Writing select(-plan) gives the same result - the minus sign means "drop this column".

5. arrange sorts the result

arrange sorts rows, ascending by default; wrap a column in desc() for descending. Chain the three verbs into one pipeline - drop basic-plan customers, keep two columns, and put the highest revenue on top:

library(dplyr)
subscriptions <- data.frame(
  customer = c("Skyline", "Nimbus", "Quartz", "Harbor"),
  plan = c("pro", "basic", "enterprise", "pro"),
  mrr = c(79, 29, 499, 129)
)
result <- subscriptions |>
  filter(plan != "basic") |>
  select(customer, mrr) |>
  arrange(desc(mrr))
print(result)

Output:

  customer mrr
1   Quartz 499
2   Harbor 129
3  Skyline  79

Pass multiple columns to arrange to handle ties: arrange(desc(mrr), customer) means sort mrr descending, and when two customers pay the same, order them by name A→Z.

Key takeaways

  • library(dplyr) must be called again at the start of every session. The "masked" messages on load are normal - this course's sandbox strips them, so you will not see them here.
  • Conditions in filter compare with == - mistyping it as = is a classic error.
  • Multiple comma-separated conditions in filter mean AND; for OR, use |.
  • arrange sorts ascending by default; for descending you must wrap the column in desc().
  • dplyr verbs never modify the original table - they return a new one. To keep the result, remember to assign it to a variable.

theory.contentHtml:
What the CEO needs is not a row-by-row customer list but the picture by plan: how many customers each plan has and how much money it brings in every month. This lesson adds the final pieces of dplyr: mutate, group_by, and summarise.

📑 Lesson contents:

  • 1. mutate adds new columns
  • 2. Grouping and aggregating with summarise
  • 3. summarise returns a tibble
  • 4. The full pipeline
  • 5. When to ungroup
  • Key takeaways

1. mutate adds new columns

mutate creates new columns from existing ones, keeping the row count unchanged. If a customer pays $79 a month, how much do they pay in a year? Multiply by 12 to get annual recurring revenue:

library(dplyr)
subscriptions <- data.frame(
  customer = c("Skyline", "Nimbus", "Quartz"),
  plan = c("pro", "basic", "enterprise"),
  mrr = c(79, 29, 499)
)
result <- subscriptions |> mutate(arr = mrr * 12)
print(result)

Output:

  customer       plan mrr  arr
1  Skyline        pro  79  948
2   Nimbus      basic  29  348
3   Quartz enterprise 499 5988

The arr column is appended on the right, and three rows are still three rows. To create several columns at once, separate them with commas.

2. Grouping and aggregating with summarise

The most powerful duo in dplyr: group_by declares "which groups to compute over", summarise declares "what to compute". The general skeleton:

data |>
  group_by(group_column) |>
  summarise(metric = aggregate_function(value_column))

group_by on its own does not change the data - it only attaches group labels. The real computation happens in summarise, using these common helpers: n() counts the rows in a group, sum() adds up, mean() averages. Count customers and total up revenue per plan:

library(dplyr)
subscriptions <- data.frame(
  customer = c("Skyline", "Nimbus", "Quartz", "Harbor", "Onyx"),
  plan = c("pro", "basic", "enterprise", "pro", "basic"),
  mrr = c(79, 29, 499, 129, 49)
)
result <- subscriptions |>
  group_by(plan) |>
  summarise(customers = n(), total_mrr = sum(mrr)) |>
  as.data.frame()
print(result)

Output:

        plan customers total_mrr
1      basic         2        78
2 enterprise         1       499
3        pro         2       208

Five customer rows collapse into three - exactly one row per group, with the groups sorted by name ascending.

3. summarise returns a tibble

Why does the pipeline above end with as.data.frame()? Because summarise does not return a regular data.frame but a tibble - the tidyverse's modern take on the data.frame. Drop the as.data.frame() and the printed result looks like this:

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  plan       customers total_mrr
  <chr>          <int>     <dbl>
1 basic              2        78
2 enterprise         1       499
3 pro                2       208

The data inside is identical; only the printing differs: an extra # A tibble line plus a row of column types. When an exercise asks you to print a plain table - and the grader compares output character by character - wrap the result in as.data.frame() before print; every practice exercise in this module follows that convention.

4. The full pipeline

Put everything you have learned together: compute the average revenue per customer for each plan, and put the plan with the biggest spenders on top:

library(dplyr)
subscriptions <- data.frame(
  customer = c("Skyline", "Nimbus", "Quartz", "Harbor", "Onyx", "Vertex"),
  plan = c("pro", "basic", "enterprise", "pro", "basic", "enterprise"),
  mrr = c(79, 29, 499, 129, 49, 899)
)
result <- subscriptions |>
  group_by(plan) |>
  summarise(customers = n(), avg_mrr = mean(mrr)) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_mrr)) |>
  as.data.frame()
print(result)

Output:

        plan customers avg_mrr
1 enterprise         2     699
2        pro         2     104
3      basic         2      39

5. When to ungroup

A mutate placed after group_by also computes per group - each row receives its own group's result. For example, attach each plan's total revenue to every customer in it:

library(dplyr)
subscriptions <- data.frame(
  customer = c("Skyline", "Nimbus", "Quartz", "Harbor"),
  plan = c("pro", "basic", "enterprise", "pro"),
  mrr = c(79, 29, 499, 129)
)
result <- subscriptions |>
  group_by(plan) |>
  mutate(plan_total = sum(mrr)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  as.data.frame()
print(result)

Output:

  customer       plan mrr plan_total
1  Skyline        pro  79        208
2   Nimbus      basic  29         29
3   Quartz enterprise 499        499
4   Harbor        pro 129        208

Both pro-plan customers get 208. ungroup() removes the group labels once the computation is done - forget it, and later steps will quietly keep running per group and produce surprising results.

Key takeaways

  • summarise collapses each group into exactly one row; mutate keeps the row count unchanged.
  • summarise returns a tibble; to print a plain table, wrap it in as.data.frame().
  • n() counts the rows in a group and takes no arguments; sum() / mean() need a column name.
  • Group labels do not disappear on their own - call ungroup() once the per-group computation is done.
  • summarise and summarize are identical; this course uses summarise.

lessons.title: Turning a summary table into a chart
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 7: Turning a summary table into a chart

theory.contentHtml:
You have just used group_by() and summarise() to boil a long table down to a few rows. But a summary table is only half the way - your manager does not read tables, they look at pictures. And so do you: one bar towering over four short ones registers before your brain has finished comparing the numbers.

ggplot2 takes the table you just summarised, exactly as it is. Nothing else to prepare.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Three pieces of every plot
  2. Feeding summarise straight into a plot
  3. Change the geom, change the chart
  4. A third dimension through colour
  5. Labels and theme
  6. Key takeaways

1. Three pieces of every plot

Every ggplot2 chart is assembled from three things, joined with +:

  • ggplot(data) - which data to use
  • aes(...) - which column goes where
  • geom_*() - what shape to draw with
library(ggplot2)

sales <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South", "Central"),
  revenue = c(320, 480, 210)
)

ggplot(sales, aes(x = region, y = revenue)) + geom_col()

Read the call in order, as a sentence: take sales, put region on the x axis and revenue on the y axis, then draw it with columns.

aes is short for aesthetic - not "aesthetic" in the decorative sense, but mapping: which column of the data corresponds to which part of the picture.

2. Feeding summarise straight into a plot

This is where ggplot2 earns its keep: the result of summarise() is a data frame, and ggplot() eats data frames. Connect them directly, with no step in between:

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

orders <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South", "North", "Central", "South", "South", "North"),
  amount = c(120, 200, 180, 90, 260, 140, 150)
)

summary_tbl <- orders %>%
  group_by(region) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(amount))

print(summary_tbl)

ggplot(summary_tbl, aes(x = region, y = total)) + geom_col(fill = "#2563eb")

The table is printed so you can check the numbers, the chart so you can see the shape. Both from one run.

To order the bars from tallest to shortest, reorder the groups with reorder() right inside aes:

library(ggplot2)

summary_tbl <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South", "Central"),
  total = c(450, 600, 90)
)

ggplot(summary_tbl, aes(x = reorder(region, -total), y = total)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2563eb")

reorder(region, -total) reads as: order region by total, the minus sign for descending.

3. Change the geom, change the chart

The power of a grammar of graphics is this: keep the data and the mapping exactly the same, swap the geom_, and you get a different kind of chart.

library(ggplot2)

trend <- data.frame(
  month = 1:6,
  revenue = c(120, 185, 240, 210, 305, 280)
)

ggplot(trend, aes(x = month, y = revenue)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2563eb", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#1e40af")

There are two geoms stacked here: a line for the trend, points marking each month. Layering is how ggplot2 works - every + geom_*() paints one more layer on top.

A quick guide:

+---------------------------------------+------------------+
|                 To see                |        Use       |
+---------------------------------------+------------------+
| A comparison across groups            | geom_col()       |
| A trend over time                     | geom_line()      |
| A relationship between two quantities | geom_point()     |
| The spread of one set of numbers      | geom_histogram() |
| The spread by group                   | geom_boxplot()   |
+---------------------------------------+------------------+

4. A third dimension through colour

aes is not limited to x and y. Mapping a column to fill adds a whole dimension of information without needing a second chart:

library(ggplot2)

sales <- data.frame(
  quarter = c("Q1", "Q1", "Q2", "Q2", "Q3", "Q3"),
  channel = c("Online", "Store", "Online", "Store", "Online", "Store"),
  revenue = c(120, 90, 180, 100, 250, 95)
)

ggplot(sales, aes(x = quarter, y = revenue, fill = channel)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge")

position = "dodge" places the two bars side by side for comparison. Drop it and they stack into a single total instead - one word changes the story the chart tells.

Notice the colour legend on the right: ggplot2 generates it for you, because you said channel maps to fill.

5. Labels and theme

labs() sets the title and axis names. theme_minimal() drops the default grey background:

library(ggplot2)

sales <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South", "Central"),
  revenue = c(320, 480, 210)
)

ggplot(sales, aes(x = region, y = revenue)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2563eb") +
  labs(
    title = "Revenue by region",
    subtitle = "Q3 2026",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Million VND"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

x = NULL removes the x axis label - when the group names already say everything, the word "region" underneath is just noise.

Key takeaways

+, not %>%. ggplot2 predates the pipe and kept + for joining layers. In one block of code you will use %>% to prepare the data and + to build the chart - mixing them up is the single most common beginner error.

Put + at the END of a line, never at the start of the next. R reads a whole line before deciding, so a line ending in + tells it more is coming. A + at the start of the next line means R already considered the statement finished.

Inside aes() means something different from outside. aes(fill = channel) means colour by the channel column - ggplot2 picks the colours and builds a legend. geom_col(fill = "#2563eb"), outside aes, means paint everything this exact colour. Getting this backwards produces a chart that is not what you wanted, for reasons that are hard to spot.

The first run of each session takes a moment. ggplot2 is downloaded to your machine the first time you call library(ggplot2), which takes a few seconds. After that it is instant.

theory.contentHtml:
Your e-commerce marketplace stores orders in one table and shipping-warehouse information in another. To answer the question "which city did order 102 ship from?", you have to join the two tables. This operation shows up in almost every real-world report, and dplyr gives you two workhorse tools: left_join() and inner_join().

📑 Lesson contents:

  • 1. Why joining tables matters
  • 2. Keeping every row of the left table
  • 3. Keeping only matching rows
  • 4. The by argument and mismatched column names
  • 5. Comparison with base R merge
  • Key takeaways

1. Why joining tables matters

Operational data rarely fits neatly into a single table. On our marketplace, the orders table records each order along with its warehouse code, while the warehouses table is a warehouse catalog with the city. The two tables talk to each other through the shared column warehouse_code:

orders <- data.frame(
  order_id = c(101, 102, 103, 104),
  warehouse_code = c("HN1", "SG1", "DN1", "HN1"),
  amount = c(250, 480, 120, 300)
)
warehouses <- data.frame(
  warehouse_code = c("HN1", "SG1"),
  city = c("Hanoi", "Ho Chi Minh")
)
print(orders)
print(warehouses)

Output:

  order_id warehouse_code amount
1      101            HN1    250
2      102            SG1    480
3      103            DN1    120
4      104            HN1    300
  warehouse_code        city
1            HN1       Hanoi
2            SG1 Ho Chi Minh

Notice a very real-life detail: order 103 shipped from warehouse DN1 - a code that does not exist in the warehouse catalog (dirty data, an everyday occurrence). How each join command handles this "orphan" row is exactly what sets them apart.

2. Keeping every row of the left table

left_join(x, y, by = "shared_col") keeps all rows of the left table x. Rows that find a match in y gain y's columns; rows with no match stay in place, and the columns taken from y receive NA:

library(dplyr)

orders <- data.frame(
  order_id = c(101, 102, 103, 104),
  warehouse_code = c("HN1", "SG1", "DN1", "HN1"),
  amount = c(250, 480, 120, 300)
)
warehouses <- data.frame(
  warehouse_code = c("HN1", "SG1"),
  city = c("Hanoi", "Ho Chi Minh")
)

result <- left_join(orders, warehouses, by = "warehouse_code") |> as.data.frame()
print(result)

Output:

  order_id warehouse_code amount        city
1      101            HN1    250       Hanoi
2      102            SG1    480 Ho Chi Minh
3      103            DN1    120        <NA>
4      104            HN1    300       Hanoi

Order 103 is still there with city as NA - the report never "drops" an order.

A quick note on |> as.data.frame(): dplyr/tidyr functions often return a tibble - the tidyverse flavor of data.frame that prints with column types and truncates rows. Tibbles are perfectly fine to use, but in this course we pipe through as.data.frame() before print() so the output is the familiar table format that is easy to compare. You will meet this pattern again in every lesson.

3. Keeping only matching rows

inner_join() is stricter: it keeps only rows that have a match in both tables. Orphan rows are dropped outright:

library(dplyr)

orders <- data.frame(
  order_id = c(101, 102, 103, 104),
  warehouse_code = c("HN1", "SG1", "DN1", "HN1"),
  amount = c(250, 480, 120, 300)
)
warehouses <- data.frame(
  warehouse_code = c("HN1", "SG1"),
  city = c("Hanoi", "Ho Chi Minh")
)

result <- inner_join(orders, warehouses, by = "warehouse_code") |> as.data.frame()
print(result)

Output:

  order_id warehouse_code amount        city
1      101            HN1    250       Hanoi
2      102            SG1    480 Ho Chi Minh
3      104            HN1    300       Hanoi

Order 103 is gone. So which one should you pick?

  • Reconciliation, revenue reports, inventory checks - every order must be present, even when lookup information is missing → left_join. The NA rows are also a valuable signal: they point at dirty data that needs handling.
  • Analysis on complete data only - for example computing average revenue per city, where rows missing a city contribute nothing → inner_join.

4. The by argument and mismatched column names

Always declare by explicitly. If you leave it out, dplyr guesses based on same-named columns and prints a message - it works, but the script will be hard to understand when you reread it three months later, and it can easily join on the wrong columns when the two tables happen to share other column names. When the two tables name their key columns differently, use the named-vector form:

left_join(x, y, by = "shared_col")
left_join(x, y, by = c("left_col" = "right_col"))

The second line reads as: column left_col of the left table matches column right_col of the right table.

5. Comparison with base R merge

In the Beginner course you met merge(). It can do the equivalent job - all.x = TRUE is exactly "keep the whole left table":

orders <- data.frame(
  order_id = c(101, 102, 103),
  warehouse_code = c("HN1", "SG1", "DN1"),
  amount = c(250, 480, 120)
)
warehouses <- data.frame(
  warehouse_code = c("HN1", "SG1"),
  city = c("Hanoi", "Ho Chi Minh")
)
merged <- merge(orders, warehouses, by = "warehouse_code", all.x = TRUE)
print(merged)

Output:

  warehouse_code order_id amount        city
1            DN1      103    120        <NA>
2            HN1      101    250       Hanoi
3            SG1      102    480 Ho Chi Minh

Compared with left_join, merge() has two surprising habits: it reorders the rows (sorting by the key column) and moves the key column to the front. left_join preserves both the row order and the column order of the left table, and it reads smoothly inside a |> pipeline - so from now on we use dplyr's *_join family as the default.

Key takeaways

  • left_join keeps the whole left table, filling non-matches with NA; inner_join keeps only rows that match on both sides. Choose based on the business question, not out of habit.
  • The row count can grow after a join: if the right table has duplicated key values (one warehouse code appearing twice), every matching left row gets duplicated. Good habit: compare nrow() before and after joining.
  • Always spell out by explicitly - don't let dplyr guess.
  • Tidyverse functions may return tibbles; to print a plain table, pipe through as.data.frame().

Your boss wants to see revenue by quarter: "one row per product, one column per quarter". But the data in the system records one product-quarter pair per row. Same data, two shapes - and tidyr gives you a pair of tools to pivot back and forth: pivot_wider() and pivot_longer().

📑 Lesson contents:

  • 1. Long data and wide data
  • 2. Pivoting from long to wide
  • 3. Filling missing values when pivoting
  • 4. Pivoting from wide back to long
  • 5. The round trip
  • Key takeaways

1. Long data and wide data

Long format: each row is one observation - one product, one quarter, one number. This is the shape systems tend to store and the shape group_by/summarise love:

revenue <- data.frame(
  product = c("Laptop", "Laptop", "Phone", "Phone"),
  quarter = c("Q1", "Q2", "Q1", "Q2"),
  revenue = c(500, 700, 300, 350)
)
print(revenue)

Output:

  product quarter revenue
1  Laptop      Q1     500
2  Laptop      Q2     700
3   Phone      Q1     300
4   Phone      Q2     350

Wide format: one row per product with the quarters spread out as columns - the shape people like to read in reports. Machines prefer long, humans prefer wide; your skill is switching between the two at the right moment.

2. Pivoting from long to wide

pivot_wider() needs two answers: where the new column names come from (names_from) and where the numbers filling the cells come from (values_from):

library(tidyr)

revenue <- data.frame(
  product = c("Laptop", "Laptop", "Phone", "Phone"),
  quarter = c("Q1", "Q2", "Q1", "Q2"),
  revenue = c(500, 700, 300, 350)
)
wide <- pivot_wider(
  revenue,
  names_from = quarter,
  values_from = revenue
) |> as.data.frame()
print(wide)

Output:

  product  Q1  Q2
1  Laptop 500 700
2   Phone 300 350

The values "Q1", "Q2" in the quarter column become column names; any column not mentioned (product) automatically serves as the row identifier. As in the previous lesson, we pipe as.data.frame() to print a plain table instead of a tibble.

3. Filling missing values when pivoting

Real life is rarely square: Laptop only sold in Q1, Phone only in Q2. When pivoting, cells with no data receive NA by default:

library(tidyr)

revenue <- data.frame(
  product = c("Laptop", "Phone"),
  quarter = c("Q1", "Q2"),
  revenue = c(500, 300)
)
wide <- pivot_wider(revenue, names_from = quarter, values_from = revenue) |> as.data.frame()
print(wide)

Output:

  product  Q1  Q2
1  Laptop 500  NA
2   Phone  NA 300

For a revenue report, "sold nothing" means 0, not "unknown". The values_fill argument captures exactly that semantics:

library(tidyr)

revenue <- data.frame(
  product = c("Laptop", "Phone"),
  quarter = c("Q1", "Q2"),
  revenue = c(500, 300)
)
wide <- pivot_wider(
  revenue,
  names_from = quarter,
  values_from = revenue,
  values_fill = 0
) |> as.data.frame()
print(wide)

Output:

  product  Q1  Q2
1  Laptop 500   0
2   Phone   0 300

But don't fill 0 mechanically: if the value column is a temperature or a survey score, missing data must stay NA - filling 0 would be fabricating numbers.

4. Pivoting from wide back to long

The opposite direction is pivot_longer(): it gathers a range of columns (cols) into two columns - the old column names go into names_to, the numbers go into values_to:

library(tidyr)

wide <- data.frame(
  product = c("Laptop", "Phone"),
  Q1 = c(500, 300),
  Q2 = c(700, 350)
)
long <- pivot_longer(
  wide,
  cols = c(Q1, Q2),
  names_to = "quarter",
  values_to = "revenue"
) |> as.data.frame()
print(long)

Output:

  product quarter revenue
1  Laptop      Q1     500
2  Laptop      Q2     700
3   Phone      Q1     300
4   Phone      Q2     350

You will use this direction a lot when you receive a "report-shaped" Excel file from another department and need to bring it back to long format for further analysis.

5. The round trip

The two functions are inverses of each other - pivoting wide and then long returns exactly the original table:

library(tidyr)

revenue <- data.frame(
  product = c("Laptop", "Laptop", "Phone", "Phone"),
  quarter = c("Q1", "Q2", "Q1", "Q2"),
  revenue = c(500, 700, 300, 350)
)
round_trip <- revenue |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = quarter, values_from = revenue) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Q1, Q2), names_to = "quarter", values_to = "revenue") |>
  as.data.frame()
print(round_trip)

Output:

  product quarter revenue
1  Laptop      Q1     500
2  Laptop      Q2     700
3   Phone      Q1     300
4   Phone      Q2     350

One exception worth remembering: if you used values_fill = 0 on the way out, the way back will carry along 0-rows that never existed in the original table - the round trip is no longer lossless.

Key takeaways

  • pivot_wider: names_from decides the new column names, values_from decides the numbers, values_fill replaces the default NA in missing combinations. Choose the fill value based on business semantics (missing revenue = 0, missing measurement = NA).
  • pivot_longer: cols selects the range of columns to gather; names_to/values_to are new column names, so write them in quotes.
  • pivot_wider requires each combination of identifier and column name to have exactly one value; if there are duplicates, tidyr warns and stuffs a list into the cell - a sign you need to summarise before pivoting.
  • Pivot results are tibbles - pipe as.data.frame() when you want to print a plain table.

theory.contentHtml:
You have just learned pivot_longer() for stretching a wide table into a long one. At the time it looked like a technical move with no obvious point - the wide table is easier to read, so why stretch it?

This lesson is the answer. Long format is exactly the shape ggplot2 needs. And once the data is long, you can split a crowded chart into a grid of small ones with a single line.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Why ggplot2 needs long data
  2. From a wide table to a chart
  3. Splitting into small panels
  4. Shared scale or free scale
  5. Key takeaways

1. Why ggplot2 needs long data

aes() maps columns onto parts of the picture. So each thing you want to draw has to be one column, not several.

This wide table is easy to read, but ggplot2 cannot use it:

wide <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South", "Central"),
  q1 = c(120, 200, 90),
  q2 = c(150, 260, 110)
)

print(wide)

Revenue is scattered across two columns, q1 and q2. To chart "revenue by quarter" you need one revenue column to map to the y axis - and there is no column here called revenue at all.

pivot_longer() gathers them:

library(tidyr)

wide <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South", "Central"),
  q1 = c(120, 200, 90),
  q2 = c(150, 260, 110)
)

long <- pivot_longer(wide, cols = c(q1, q2), names_to = "quarter", values_to = "revenue")
print(long)

Now you have exactly what you need: a quarter column saying which quarter, a revenue column saying how much. Six rows instead of three, but this is the shape a machine can read.

2. From a wide table to a chart

Chain the whole thing together - pivot, then draw:

library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

wide <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South", "Central"),
  q1 = c(120, 200, 90),
  q2 = c(150, 260, 110)
)

long <- pivot_longer(wide, cols = c(q1, q2), names_to = "quarter", values_to = "revenue")

ggplot(long, aes(x = region, y = revenue, fill = quarter)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Revenue by region and quarter", y = "Million VND", x = NULL)

The quarter column - the one pivot_longer just created - is what goes into fill. Without the pivot there would be no such column to map.

3. Splitting into small panels

As the number of groups grows, cramming them all into one chart turns it into a mess. facet_wrap() splits it into small panels, one per group:

library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

wide <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South", "Central"),
  q1 = c(120, 200, 90),
  q2 = c(150, 260, 110),
  q3 = c(180, 240, 130),
  q4 = c(210, 300, 95)
)

long <- pivot_longer(wide, cols = q1:q4, names_to = "quarter", values_to = "revenue")

ggplot(long, aes(x = quarter, y = revenue)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2563eb") +
  facet_wrap(~ region) +
  labs(title = "Revenue trend by region", y = "Million VND", x = NULL)

The ~ reads as "by": facet_wrap(~ region) means split by region. Three regions become three panels, each telling its own story, placed side by side for comparison.

This reads far faster than three colours overlaid in one frame - the eye never has to hunt through a legend.

4. Shared scale or free scale

By default every panel uses the same axis scale. That is usually what you want, because comparison between panels only means anything when the scales match.

But when the groups differ wildly, the small one gets flattened into a straight line. That is when you give each panel its own scale:

library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

wide <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South"),
  q1 = c(20, 2000),
  q2 = c(35, 2600)
)

long <- pivot_longer(wide, cols = c(q1, q2), names_to = "quarter", values_to = "revenue")

ggplot(long, aes(x = quarter, y = revenue)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2563eb") +
  facet_wrap(~ region, scales = "free_y")

scales = "free_y" lets the y axis of each panel size itself. Try removing that line and running it again: North all but disappears, crushed by South.

This is a double-edged tool. Free scales make the shape of the small group visible, but viewers very easily read two equally tall bars as two equal values. If you use it, say so in the title.

Key takeaways

Long format is for the machine, not the reader. A wide table is still better when printed for people. The common workflow is: keep the table wide for reporting, pivot_longer right before drawing.

facet_wrap is not fill. Same data, two ways of telling it: fill overlays the groups in one frame for direct comparison; facet_wrap separates them so each gets its own space. Few groups and a need for precise comparison - use fill; many groups, or each with its own shape - facet_wrap.

Be careful with scales = "free". It solves the flattening problem and creates a misreading problem. The shared scale is the right default - change it only when you have a reason, and state that reason.

headings.text: 2. From a wide table to a chart

questions.prompt: You join the orders table (left) with the warehouse catalog (right) using left_join on the warehouse code. One order has a warehouse code that does not exist in the catalog. What happens to that row?

options.label: A
options.text: That order row is dropped from the result

options.label: B
options.text: The row is kept, and the columns taken from the warehouse table receive NA

options.label: C
options.text: R throws an error because no matching value is found

options.label: D
options.text: The city column receives an empty string ""

questions.explanation: left_join keeps every row of the left table. Rows with no match stay in the result, with the columns coming from the right table set to NA - so the report never drops an order.

questions.prompt: What is the core difference of inner_join compared with left_join?

options.label: A
options.text: inner_join runs faster, so it is always preferred

options.label: B
options.text: inner_join keeps only rows that have a match in both tables

options.label: C
options.text: inner_join keeps all rows of both tables

options.label: D
options.text: inner_join reorders the columns while left_join does not

questions.explanation: inner_join is an intersection: a row must match in both tables to be kept. Orphan rows in the left table (which left_join keeps with NA) are dropped by inner_join.

questions.prompt: orders has 100 rows. In warehouses, the code "HN1" accidentally appears twice. How many rows does left_join(orders, warehouses, by = "warehouse_code") return?

options.label: A
options.text: Always exactly 100 rows, left_join never changes the row count

options.label: B
options.text: Possibly more than 100 rows, because every left row matching the duplicated code gets duplicated

options.label: C
options.text: Always fewer than 100 rows because duplicate rows are merged

options.label: D
options.text: R automatically removes the duplicate record in warehouses before joining

questions.explanation: A duplicated key in the right table makes every matching left row get multiplied by the number of duplicates - the result silently balloons. Good habit: compare nrow() before and after joining.

questions.prompt: In pivot_wider, which argument decides the NAMES of the newly created columns?

options.label: A
options.text: values_from

options.label: B
options.text: values_fill

options.label: C
options.text: names_from

options.label: D
options.text: cols

questions.explanation: names_from specifies the column whose values (Q1, Q2, ...) become the new column names; values_from specifies the column holding the numbers that fill the cells; values_fill only fills the gaps.

questions.prompt: When pivot_wider meets a product-quarter combination that does not exist in the data, what value does that cell receive by default?

options.label: B
options.text: NA

options.label: C
options.text: An empty string

options.label: D
options.text: That product row is dropped from the result

questions.explanation: The default is NA. To fill a different value (for example 0 for revenue), use values_fill = 0 - but only when the business semantics allow treating missing data as a true zero.

questions.prompt: With pivot_longer(wide, cols = c(Q1, Q2), names_to = "quarter", values_to = "revenue"), where do the two column names Q1 and Q2 end up?

options.label: A
options.text: They become values in the quarter column

options.label: B
options.text: They become values in the revenue column

options.label: C
options.text: They are deleted entirely, leaving no trace in the result

options.label: D
options.text: They become the row names of the resulting table

questions.explanation: names_to receives the NAMES of the old columns as values ("Q1", "Q2" go into the quarter column), while values_to receives the numbers inside those columns (going into the revenue column).

questions.prompt: You have a wide table region | q1 | q2 | q3. Why must you pivot_longer() before charting revenue by quarter with ggplot2?

options.label: A
options.text: Because long tables are smaller

options.label: B
options.text: Because aes() maps columns onto axes, and revenue is scattered across several columns

options.label: C
options.text: Because ggplot2 cannot read a data.frame

options.label: D
options.text: Because the quarters need reordering

questions.explanation: Each thing you want to draw has to be one column. The wide table has no column called revenue - it is spread across q1, q2, q3. pivot_longer() gathers them into one value column and one label column.

questions.prompt: What is the risk with facet_wrap(~ region, scales = "free_y")?

options.label: A
options.text: It draws noticeably slower

options.label: B
options.text: Viewers easily read two equally tall bars as two equal values

options.label: C
options.text: The colour legend disappears

options.label: D
options.text: It cannot be used with geom_col

questions.explanation: Free scales make the shape of a small group visible, but each panel has its own scale, so comparing heights across panels compares the wrong thing. The shared scale is the right default - say so in the title if you change it.

practice.title: Reconciling orders with warehouses
practice.summaryHtml: The marketplace operations team needs an end-of-day reconciliation table: every order must clearly show which city it shipped from, and absolutely no order may be left out - including orders entered with a bad warehouse code.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.html:
Write a function orders_with_warehouse(orders, warehouses) that takes two tables:

  • orders - one row per order: order_id (order code), warehouse_code (code of the shipping warehouse), amount (order value).
  • warehouses - the warehouse catalog: warehouse_code (warehouse code), city (city where the warehouse is located).

Return a data.frame with exactly 3 columns in this order:

  • order_id: the order code.
  • city: the city of the warehouse that shipped the order.
  • amount: the order value.

Business constraints:

  • Every order must appear in the report, including orders whose warehouse cannot be identified (warehouse code not in the catalog) - in that case leave city empty (NA).
  • A warehouse with no orders must not add any rows to the report.
  • Sort by order_id ascending.

sections.title: Example 1
sections.html:
Input:

orders <- data.frame(
  order_id = c(3, 1, 2),
  warehouse_code = c("HN1", "SG2", "HN1"),
  amount = c(150, 900, 420)
)
warehouses <- data.frame(
  warehouse_code = c("HN1", "SG2"),
  city = c("Hanoi", "Springfield")
)
print(orders_with_warehouse(orders, warehouses))

Output:

  order_id        city amount
1        1 Springfield    900
2        2       Hanoi    420
3        3       Hanoi    150

sections.title: Example 2
sections.html:
Input:

orders <- data.frame(
  order_id = c(10, 11),
  warehouse_code = c("DN1", "XX9"),
  amount = c(75.5, 200)
)
warehouses <- data.frame(
  warehouse_code = c("DN1", "CT1"),
  city = c("Denver", "Cleveland")
)
print(orders_with_warehouse(orders, warehouses))

Output:

  order_id    city amount
1       10 Denver   75.5
2       11    <NA>  200.0

Order 11 was entered with warehouse code XX9, which is not in the catalog, yet it must still appear with city as NA; warehouse CT1 has no orders, so it produces no row.

  order_id = c(3, 1, 2),
  warehouse_code = c("HN1", "SG2", "HN1"),
  amount = c(150, 900, 420)
)
warehouses <- data.frame(
  warehouse_code = c("HN1", "SG2"),
  city = c("Hanoi", "Springfield")
)
print(orders_with_warehouse(orders, warehouses))

theory.contentHtml:
The marketing team just pulled in 5,000 customer emails from three sources: the sign-up form on the website, a reseller's Excel file, and a list of QR-code scans from an offline event. Open the file and look: UPPERCASE here, lowercase there, stray whitespace all over the place, and every source formats product SKU codes its own way. Before running any campaign, you have to clean the strings - and stringr is the toolkit designed for exactly this job.

📑 Lesson contents:

  • 1. Loading stringr
  • 2. Changing case
  • 3. Trimming whitespace and measuring length
  • 4. Finding and replacing
  • 5. Extracting substrings
  • 6. Compared with the base R you already know

1. Loading stringr

stringr is the string-processing package of the tidyverse ecosystem. Every function starts with the str_ prefix, takes the string as its first argument, and runs on whole vectors - the names are easy to guess and the code is easy to read.

library(stringr)

str_to_upper("hello data team")

Output:

[1] "HELLO DATA TEAM"

💡 The sandbox installs stringr automatically when it sees library(stringr) - the first run takes a few seconds, later runs are back to normal speed.

2. Changing case

Email addresses are case-insensitive, but to R "AN@SHOP.VN" and "an@shop.vn" are two different strings. The first step in cleaning text data is always to bring everything to one standard: emails to lowercase, SKU codes to uppercase.

library(stringr)

emails <- c("An.NGUYEN@Shop.vn", "BINH@SHOP.VN")
str_to_lower(emails)

sku <- c("gh-1024-xl", "tv-88-s")
str_to_upper(sku)

Output:

[1] "an.nguyen@shop.vn" "binh@shop.vn"
[1] "GH-1024-XL" "TV-88-S"

Both functions are vectorized: feed in a vector of 5,000 elements and all 5,000 get processed - no loop needed.

3. Trimming whitespace and measuring length

Stray whitespace at the start and end of a string is the most common bug when users type into forms. str_trim() cuts both ends clean, and str_length() counts characters - a handy pair for spotting dirty data.

library(stringr)

raw <- c("  minh.tran@mail.com  ", "lan.pham@mail.com")
cleaned <- str_trim(raw)
cleaned
str_length(cleaned)

Output:

[1] "minh.tran@mail.com" "lan.pham@mail.com"
[1] 18 17

The first string drops from 22 characters (whitespace included) to 18 - exactly the "meat" of the email.

4. Finding and replacing

str_detect(string, pattern) returns TRUE/FALSE for each element - use it for filtering. For example: which rows in the contact list actually contain an @ character?

library(stringr)

contacts <- c("thu.le@shop.vn", "walk in customer", "vy@shop.vn")
str_detect(contacts, "@")

Output:

[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE

Meanwhile str_replace() replaces the first occurrence of the pattern and str_replace_all() replaces all of them - a difference that is very easy to forget:

library(stringr)

typo <- c("binh@gmall.com", "an@gmall.com")
str_replace(typo, "gmall", "gmail")

sku <- "TV 88 S"
str_replace(sku, " ", "-")
str_replace_all(sku, " ", "-")

Output:

[1] "binh@gmail.com" "an@gmail.com"
[1] "TV-88 S"
[1] "TV-88-S"

The string "TV 88 S" has two spaces: str_replace() only fixes the first one - you need str_replace_all() to get a proper SKU code.

5. Extracting substrings

str_sub(string, start, end) grabs a slice by character position. Its winning edge over base R's substr(): it accepts negative indices that count backwards from the end of the string.

library(stringr)

sku <- c("TV-88-S", "GH-1024-XL")
str_sub(sku, 1, 2)
str_sub(sku, -2, -1)

Output:

[1] "TV" "GH"
[1] "-S" "XL"

The first two characters are the category code and the last two are the size - even though the codes differ in length, negative indices still grab the right part.

6. Compared with the base R you already know

In the Beginner course you already met base R's string functions. They still work fine - stringr does not replace them, it standardizes the interface:

+---------------------+-----------------------+----------------------------------+
|         Task        |         base R        |              stringr             |
+---------------------+-----------------------+----------------------------------+
| Lowercase           | tolower(x)            | str_to_lower(x)                  |
| Trim whitespace     | trimws(x)             | str_trim(x)                      |
| Count characters    | nchar(x)              | str_length(x)                    |
| Detect a pattern    | grepl(pattern, x)     | str_detect(x, pattern)           |
| Replace all         | gsub(pattern, new, x) | str_replace_all(x, pattern, new) |
| Extract a substring | substr(x, start, end) | str_sub(x, start, end)           |
+---------------------+-----------------------+----------------------------------+

Mind the biggest trap of all: argument order. Base R puts the pattern first (grepl("@", emails)), stringr puts the string first (str_detect(emails, "@")). The results are exactly the same:

library(stringr)

emails <- c("an@shop.vn", "no email")
grepl("@", emails)
str_detect(emails, "@")

Output:

[1]  TRUE FALSE
[1]  TRUE FALSE

Key takeaways

  • library(stringr) must run before calling any str_* function. In the sandbox, the first load installs the package automatically - waiting a few seconds is normal.
  • Every str_* function takes the string as the first argument, the pattern after it - the reverse of grepl()/gsub(). Switching between the two styles is an easy way to slip up.
  • str_replace() only replaces the first occurrence; to replace them all, use str_replace_all().
  • All these functions are vectorized - don't write a for loop to process string elements one at a time.

theory.contentHtml:
The email list is clean, but now your manager follows up: "How many of these emails actually belong to the shop.vn domain? And pull the numeric part out of SKU codes like GH-1024-XL while you're at it." A literal string like "shop.vn" cannot express the idea of "one or more digits" - you need regex (regular expressions), a language purpose-built for describing string patterns.

📑 Lesson contents:

  • 1. Literals and patterns
  • 2. Character classes in square brackets
  • 3. The dot and quantifiers
  • 4. Anchoring the start and end of a string
  • 5. Shorthand and double escaping
  • 6. Filtering emails and extracting SKU numbers

1. Literals and patterns

In the previous lesson, the second argument of str_detect() was a literal string - it matched exactly the characters you typed:

library(stringr)

emails <- c("an@shop.vn", "binh@gmail.com", "chi@shop.vn")
str_detect(emails, "shop")

Output:

[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE

In fact that argument is always interpreted as a pattern (a regex). When a string holds nothing but letters and digits, the pattern equals the literal; the power lies in the special characters that describe the "shape" of a string rather than its exact content.

2. Character classes in square brackets

[0-9] means "any ONE character in the range 0 to 9". Likewise, [a-z] is any single lowercase letter:

library(stringr)

sku <- c("TV-88", "GH-XL", "AC-07")
str_detect(sku, "[0-9]")

Output:

[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE

"GH-XL" contains no digits, so it is FALSE. Note that regex is case-sensitive: [a-z] matches "abc" but not "ABC" - to accept both, write [a-zA-Z].

3. The dot and quantifiers

The dot . in regex means "any ONE character" - a classic source of bugs when checking email domains:

library(stringr)

domains <- c("shop.vn", "shopxvn", "shop-vn")
str_detect(domains, "shop.vn")

Output:

[1] TRUE TRUE TRUE

All three are TRUE! The pattern "shop.vn" also matches "shopxvn" because . happily swallows the character x. How to write a "real" dot comes in section 5.

Quantifiers follow a pattern to say how many times it repeats: + means "one or more times", * means "zero times is fine too":

library(stringr)

x <- c("ab", "acb", "accb")
str_detect(x, "ac+b")
str_detect(x, "ac*b")

Output:

[1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE
[1] TRUE TRUE TRUE

"ac+b" demands at least one c, so "ab" fails; "ac*b" accepts having no c at all. Combined with a character class, [0-9]+ means "a run of consecutive digits" - exactly the numeric part of an SKU code:

library(stringr)

sku <- c("GH-1024-XL", "TV-88-S")
str_replace_all(sku, "[0-9]+", "N")

Output:

[1] "GH-N-XL" "TV-N-S"

4. Anchoring the start and end of a string

By default str_detect() only needs the pattern to appear somewhere in the string. To pin down the position, use anchors: ^ for the start of the string, $ for the end.

library(stringr)

sku <- c("TV-88", "88-TV", "TV88")
str_detect(sku, "^TV")

Output:

[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE

Filtering emails by domain is the textbook $ use case - the domain must sit at the end of the address:

library(stringr)

emails <- c("an@shop.vn", "shop.vn@gmail.com", "chi@shop.vn")
str_detect(emails, "shop\\.vn$")

Output:

[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE

"shop.vn@gmail.com" contains shop.vn but not at the end of the string → rejected, exactly as intended.

5. Shorthand and double escaping

Regex has shorthand notation: \d is equivalent to [0-9]. But in R the pattern is written inside a string, and R strings also use \ as their escape character - so you have to type two backslashes:

# Wrong - R stops with: '\d' is an unrecognized escape in character string
str_detect(sku, "\d")

R's string layer "eats" one of the backslashes; write "\\d" and what actually reaches the regex engine is \d:

library(stringr)

sku <- c("GH-1024-XL", "TV-88-S")
str_detect(sku, "\\d")

Output:

[1] TRUE TRUE

This rule applies to every special character you want taken literally. The "real" dot from section 3 is written "\\.":

library(stringr)

domains <- c("shop.vn", "shopxvn")
str_detect(domains, "shop\\.vn")

Output:

[1]  TRUE FALSE

This time "shopxvn" has no way to slip through.

6. Filtering emails and extracting SKU numbers

Time to put it all together. A valid internal shop.vn email: from the start up to the @ there are only lowercase letters, digits or dots, and the whole string ends with @shop.vn:

library(stringr)

emails <- c("an@shop.vn", "  binh@shop.vn", "chi@@shop.vn", "vy@shop.vn")
str_detect(emails, "^[a-z0-9.]+@shop\\.vn$")

Output:

[1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE  TRUE

The email with leading whitespace fails the ^ anchor, and the one with two @ characters does not match the structure - both get dropped. (Inside [a-z0-9.] the dot sits within square brackets, so it is automatically literal - no escape needed.)

And pulling the number out of an SKU code? Delete every character that is not a digit - [^0-9], with the caret first inside the square brackets, means "a character NOT in this class":

library(stringr)

sku <- c("GH-1024-XL", "TV-88-S")
str_replace_all(sku, "[^0-9]", "")

Output:

[1] "1024" "88"

Key takeaways

  • Two layers of escaping: when the regex needs \., the R string must be written "\\."; when the regex needs \d, write "\\d". One missing backslash means either a syntax error or a silently wrong match.
  • A bare . matches every character - checking a domain while forgetting to escape the dot lets dirty data through.
  • str_detect() matches a part of the string by default; to match the whole string, anchor with both ^ and $.
  • Quick reference: [0-9] a digit, [a-z] a lowercase letter, . any character, + repeats one or more times, * repeats zero or more times, ^ start of string, $ end of string, \d shorthand for [0-9].

questions.prompt: What does str_trim(" ha@shop.vn ") return?

options.label: A
options.text: " ha@shop.vn" - only trims the trailing whitespace

options.label: B
options.text: "ha@shop.vn" - trims the whitespace at both ends

options.label: C
options.text: "ha@shop.vn " - only trims the leading whitespace

options.label: D
options.text: "hashop.vn" - strips the special characters too

questions.explanation: str_trim() removes stray whitespace at BOTH ends of the string and never touches any character in the middle.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between str_replace() and str_replace_all()?

options.label: A
options.text: str_replace() runs faster but the results are always identical

options.label: B
options.text: str_replace_all() works on vectors, str_replace() only accepts a single string

options.label: C
options.text: str_replace() only replaces the first occurrence, str_replace_all() replaces all of them

options.label: D
options.text: str_replace_all() replaces both the uppercase and lowercase forms of the pattern

questions.explanation: When the same pattern appears several times in one string: str_replace() stops after the first hit, str_replace_all() sweeps through all of them. Both are vectorized.

questions.prompt: The base R call grepl("@", emails) is equivalent to which stringr call?

options.label: A
options.text: str_detect(emails, "@")

options.label: B
options.text: str_detect("@", emails)

options.label: C
options.text: str_replace(emails, "@")

options.label: D
options.text: str_sub(emails, "@")

questions.explanation: Both functions return TRUE/FALSE per element, but the argument order is reversed: grepl(pattern, string) versus stringr, which always takes the string first and the pattern second.

questions.prompt: Which part of the string "GH-1024-XL" does the pattern "[0-9]+" match?

options.label: A
options.text: Only the first digit, i.e. 1

options.label: B
options.text: The whole string, because it contains digits

options.label: C
options.text: GH, because it sits at the start of the string

options.label: D
options.text: The whole run 1024, because + means one or more consecutive digits

questions.explanation: [0-9] matches ONE digit; adding the quantifier + matches the longest possible run of consecutive digits - here that is 1024.

questions.prompt: To use the regex shorthand \d (one digit) in R, how must the pattern be written?

options.label: A
options.text: "\d" - written exactly like the regex

options.label: B
options.text: "\\d" - two backslashes

options.label: C
options.text: "d" - R automatically reads d as a digit

options.label: D
options.text: "//d" - using forward slashes

questions.explanation: Strings in R also use the backslash as an escape character, so it "eats" one of them. Write "\\d" and what actually reaches the regex engine is \d; write "\d" and R reports an unrecognized escape error.

questions.prompt: str_detect(emails, "@shop\\.vn$") returns TRUE for which emails?

options.label: A
options.text: Emails containing @shop anywhere in the string

options.label: B
options.text: Emails starting with @shop.vn

options.label: C
options.text: Emails ending with @shop.vn, where the dot is a real dot

options.label: D
options.text: Emails with exactly one arbitrary character between shop and vn

questions.explanation: $ anchors the pattern to the end of the string, and \\. is an escaped dot that only matches a real dot - both shopxvn and shop.vn@gmail.com are rejected.

practice.title: Cleaning up an email list
practice.summaryHtml: Mai, the marketing team lead, sends you an exported list of customer emails, gathered from the website form, resellers' files and the event booth. Her note: "This list is really messy - UPPERCASE mixed with lowercase, stray spaces everywhere, plus blank lines and rows that aren't emails at all. Please filter it into a clean list for me so we can run the campaign next week."

sections.title: Requirements
sections.html:
Write a function clean_emails(email_vec) that takes a character vector of raw emails and returns a character vector of valid, normalized emails:

  • Normalize each element: trim stray whitespace at both ends, convert everything to lowercase.
  • An element (after normalization) counts as a valid email when: it contains exactly one @ character, and there is at least one dot after the @.
  • Invalid elements (empty string, missing @, extra @, no dot after the @, ...) are dropped from the result.
  • Remove duplicates: after normalization, if two elements are identical, keep only one.
  • Sort the result alphabetically from A to Z.

The result is printed with cat(clean_emails(...), sep = "\n") - the output is plain text, one email per line, no [1], no quotes. If no email is valid, print nothing at all.

sections.title: Example 1
sections.html:
Input: cat(clean_emails(c(" Aaron.Nelson@Shop.vn", "brian@shop.vn ", "no email here")), sep = "\n")

Output:

an.nguyen@shop.vn
brian@shop.vn

sections.title: Example 2
sections.html:
Input: cat(clean_emails(c("VERA@shop.vn", "vera@shop.vn ", "chi@shopvn")), sep = "\n")

Output:

vera@shop.vn

lessons.title: Dates with as.Date and difftime
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 21: Dates with as.Date and difftime

theory.contentHtml:
You are an operations specialist at a delivery company. Every day the system pours in thousands of orders with an order date (order_date) and a delivery date (delivered_date), and your boss only ever asks three questions: how many days does an average order take, which month has slower deliveries, and which orders missed the promised deadline? To answer them, the first step is teaching R that the string "2026-03-15" is a date, not just a sequence of characters.

📑 Lesson contents:

  • 1. Converting strings to dates
  • 2. Vietnamese date format
  • 3. The gap between two dates
  • 4. Comparing dates against a promised deadline
  • 5. Grouping orders by month
  • 6. Date sequences, earliest and latest dates

1. Converting strings to dates

as.Date() is the doorway that brings date data into R. With a string in the standard year-month-day form "YYYY-MM-DD", just call it directly:

order_date <- as.Date("2026-03-15")
print(order_date)
print(class(order_date))

Output:

[1] "2026-03-15"
[1] "Date"

It still looks like a string, but class shows this is a Date object - from now on R adds, subtracts, compares, and sorts it with proper calendar logic.

2. Vietnamese date format

Files from the warehouse often record "15/03/2026" (day/month/year). Feeding that straight into as.Date() errors out or returns NA - you must declare a format describing the string's structure:

vn_date <- as.Date("15/03/2026", format = "%d/%m/%Y")
print(vn_date)

Output:

[1] "2026-03-15"

Here %d is the day, %m is the month, and %Y is the 4-digit year. The / must match the separator used in the string exactly.

3. The gap between two dates

Subtract one Date from another and R returns a difftime object:

order_date <- as.Date("2026-03-11")
delivered_date <- as.Date("2026-03-15")
gap <- delivered_date - order_date
print(gap)
print(as.numeric(gap))

Output:

Time difference of 4 days
[1] 4

difftime prints nicely, but for further computation (averages, sums, threshold comparisons) convert it to a number with as.numeric(). The subtraction works on whole vectors too - one difference per order:

order_dates <- as.Date(c("2026-03-01", "2026-03-03"))
delivered_dates <- as.Date(c("2026-03-04", "2026-03-04"))
gaps <- as.numeric(delivered_dates - order_dates)
print(gaps)
print(mean(gaps))

Output:

[1] 3 1
[1] 2

The last two lines are the core of every "average delivery time" report.

4. Comparing dates against a promised deadline

Date values can be compared with the familiar operators <, >, <=, >=. An order delivered after the promised date is late:

delivered_date <- as.Date("2026-03-15")
promised_date <- as.Date("2026-03-14")
is_late <- delivered_date > promised_date
print(is_late)
print(delivered_date < as.Date("2026-04-01"))

Output:

[1] TRUE
[1] TRUE

Combined with what you know about vector filtering, you can count late orders in a single line: sum(delivered > promised).

5. Grouping orders by month

Monthly reports need a "month key" derived from each date. format() with the pattern "%Y-%m" cuts out exactly the year-month part:

delivered_dates <- as.Date(c("2026-01-28", "2026-02-03", "2026-02-15"))
month_key <- format(delivered_dates, "%Y-%m")
print(month_key)
print(sum(month_key == "2026-02"))

Output:

[1] "2026-01" "2026-02" "2026-02"
[1] 2

month_key is a character vector - handy for filtering, counting, or grouping data by month.

6. Date sequences, earliest and latest dates

seq() creates a sequence of consecutive dates (useful when you need to scan day by day for orders), while min() / max() find the earliest and latest dates:

march_days <- seq(as.Date("2026-03-01"), as.Date("2026-03-05"), by = "day")
print(march_days)
print(min(march_days))
print(max(march_days))

Output:

[1] "2026-03-01" "2026-03-02" "2026-03-03" "2026-03-04" "2026-03-05"
[1] "2026-03-01"
[1] "2026-03-05"

Key takeaways

  • By default as.Date() only understands the year-month-day form ("2026-03-15" or "2026/03/15"). Vietnamese-style strings must come with format = "%d/%m/%Y".
  • Subtracting two Date values yields a difftime - pleasant to read but awkward to compute with. Good habit: wrap it in as.numeric() as soon as you need the number.
  • Never compare dates while they are still free-form strings: "5/3/2026" > "14/2/2026" compares alphabetically and the result is meaningless. Always convert to Date first.
  • R ships with weekdays() and months(), which return the names of weekdays/months, but those names change with each machine's system language (an English machine prints "Sunday", another machine prints something else). The lessons and graders in this course do not use those two functions - when you need month information, use format(date, "%Y-%m") or "%m" for results that are stable on every machine.
