questions.prompt: Running class(as.Date("2026-05-01")) in R, what is the returned result?

options.label: A
options.text: "character"

options.label: B
options.text: "Date"

options.label: C
options.text: "numeric"

options.label: D
options.text: "difftime"

questions.explanation: as.Date() converts a string into an object of class Date. That is what lets R add, subtract, compare, and sort by proper calendar logic - a character string cannot.

questions.prompt: The warehouse team records dates the Vietnamese way: "05/03/2026" (day/month/year). Which command correctly converts this string into March 5, 2026?
questions.explanation: The string is not in year-month-day form, so you must declare the format: %d is the day, %m is the month, %Y is the 4-digit year. Option b reads 05 as month 5 (giving May 3, 2026), and format() only prints a date as a string - it does not parse one.

questions.prompt: What line does print(as.Date("2026-04-10") - as.Date("2026-04-03")) print to the screen?

options.label: A
options.text: Time difference of 7 days

options.label: C
options.text: [1] "7 days"

options.label: D
options.text: An error because two dates cannot be subtracted

questions.explanation: Subtracting two Date objects returns a difftime object, printed as the sentence "Time difference of ... days". To get the bare number 7 for further computation, you must wrap it in as.numeric().

questions.prompt: You have gap <- as.Date("2026-06-09") - as.Date("2026-06-02") and need the plain number 7 to average together with other orders. What is the standard way?

options.label: A
options.text: as.character(gap)

options.label: B
options.text: print(gap)

options.label: C
options.text: as.numeric(gap)

options.label: D
options.text: format(gap, "%d")

questions.explanation: as.numeric() converts a difftime into the number of days as a numeric value so that mean() and sum() work as expected. as.character() produces a string, and print() only prints - it does not change the type.

questions.prompt: To group delivery orders by month, what value does format(as.Date("2026-12-25"), "%Y-%m") return?
questions.explanation: %Y takes the 4-digit year, %m takes the 2-digit month, joined by a dash exactly as in the pattern - the result "2026-12" makes a very convenient key for grouping by month.

questions.prompt: How many elements are in the date vector created by seq(as.Date("2026-01-01"), as.Date("2026-01-04"), by = "day")?
questions.explanation: The sequence includes both the first and the last day: January 01, 02, 03, and 04 - 4 days in total.

practice.title: Average delivery time
practice.summaryHtml: The head of operations needs one single number for the weekly report: on average, how many days does an order take from the moment the customer places it until it is successfully delivered.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.html:
Write a function avg_delivery_days(order_dates, delivered_dates) where:

  • order_dates is a vector of order-date strings and delivered_dates is a vector of successful-delivery-date strings - both in year-month-day form (e.g. "2026-01-02") and parallel per order: the i-th elements of the two vectors belong to the same order.
  • The function returns a single number: the average delivery time in days across all orders (delivery date minus order date), rounded to 1 decimal place. An order delivered on the very day it was placed counts as 0 days.
  • The grader prints the result via cat(...), so the output is bare text with no leading [1]. Following R's printing rules: if the rounded value is a whole number it prints compactly with no decimal part (2, not 2.0); otherwise it prints in full (2.5).

sections.title: Example 1
sections.html:
Input: cat(avg_delivery_days(c("2026-01-02", "2026-01-05"), c("2026-01-05", "2026-01-06")))

Output:

2

sections.title: Example 2
sections.html:
Input: cat(avg_delivery_days(c("2026-02-01", "2026-02-10"), c("2026-02-04", "2026-02-12")))

Output:

2.5

theory.contentHtml:
The HR team sends you an employee dataset along with two familiar questions: "Does salary really grow with tenure?" and "Which departments is headcount piling into?". A feeling that "it seems so" is not enough for a report - People Analytics needs numbers. This lesson equips you with two lightweight R tools: cor() to measure how strongly two metrics are related, and table() together with prop.table() to count and then turn counts into proportions.

📑 Lesson contents:

  • 1. The correlation coefficient between two metrics
  • 2. One-way frequency tables
  • 3. Two-way frequency tables
  • 4. Turning counts into percentages
  • Key takeaways

1. The correlation coefficient between two metrics

cor(x, y) takes two numeric vectors of the same length and returns the correlation coefficient - a number that always falls between -1 and 1:

  • Close to 1: the two metrics rise and fall together (strong positive relationship).
  • Close to -1: when one goes up, the other goes down (strong negative relationship).
  • Close to 0: almost no linear relationship.

Try it with salary data that climbs perfectly in step with tenure:

tenure <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
salary <- c(12, 14, 16, 18, 20)
cat(round(cor(tenure, salary), 2), "\n")

Output:

1

Each extra year of tenure adds exactly 2 million to the salary - a perfect linear relationship, so cor is exactly 1. Real data is rarely that pretty:

tenure <- c(1, 2, 3)
salary <- c(10, 20, 40)
cat(round(cor(tenure, salary), 2), "\n")

Output:

0.98

Salary still grows with tenure but unevenly (later steps jump faster than earlier ones), so cor is very high without reaching 1. And when the relationship is negative, the value goes below zero:

overtime <- c(1, 2, 3)
satisfaction <- c(4, 2, 1)
cat(round(cor(overtime, satisfaction), 2), "\n")

Output:

-0.98

A habit worth keeping: calling cor() bare prints a long-winded number like [1] 0.9819805 - when putting it into a report, wrap it in round(..., 2) (or 3 digits) and print it with cat() to keep things tidy.

2. One-way frequency tables

table() counts how many times each value appears - exactly the question "how many people are in each department":

dept <- c("Sales", "IT", "Sales", "HR")
print(table(dept))

Output:

dept
   HR    IT Sales
    1     1     2

The top row lists the values that appear in the data, the bottom row the counts: 1 person in HR, 1 in IT, 2 in Sales.

3. Two-way frequency tables

Pass two vectors of the same length to cross-count - for example, department structure by seniority level:

dept <- c("Sales", "IT", "Sales", "HR")
level <- c("Junior", "Senior", "Senior", "Junior")
print(table(level, dept))

Output:

        dept
level    HR IT Sales
  Junior  1  0     1
  Senior  0  1     1

Read it cell by cell: 1 Junior in HR, 1 Junior in Sales, 1 Senior in IT, 1 Senior in Sales. Cross tables like this are the opening move of most workforce-structure analyses.

4. Turning counts into percentages

Your boss rarely asks "how many people" - the boss asks "what percentage". prop.table() takes the result of table() and divides each cell by the total; multiply by 100 and round to get percentages:

dept <- c("Sales", "IT", "Sales", "HR")
print(round(prop.table(table(dept)) * 100))

Output:

dept
   HR    IT Sales
   25    25    50

Sales makes up half the headcount - a number you can drop straight into a slide.

Key takeaways

  • cor() only measures linear relationships. A U-shaped relationship can give a cor near 0 even though the two metrics are tightly linked.
  • Correlation is not causation: salary and tenure moving together does not mean one causes the other.
  • prop.table() is applied to the result of table(), not directly to the raw vector.
  • Always round before putting numbers into a report - nobody wants to read 0.9819805.

lessons.title: Comparing two groups with t.test
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 25: Comparing two groups with t.test

theory.contentHtml:
You compare the average salary at two offices: Hanoi 51.17 million, Ho Chi Minh City 54 million. The head of HR asks right away: "Almost a 3 million gap - is that a real difference, or did this round of sampling just get lucky?". The question "is the difference significant" shows up everywhere: comparing salaries across two offices, comparing conversion between two landing page variants, comparing satisfaction scores before and after a new policy. R answers it with a single function: t.test() - no math formulas to memorize.

📑 Lesson contents:

  • 1. Asking whether a difference is significant
  • 2. Running the test on two groups
  • 3. Reading the test results
  • 4. The decision threshold and how to conclude
  • Key takeaways

1. Asking whether a difference is significant

Two groups of measurements almost always differ a little - even when there is truly nothing different about them, simply because samples are random. A two-sample test settles the question: it returns a p-value - the probability of observing a gap this large (or larger) if the two groups were actually no different. The smaller p is, the harder the gap becomes to blame on luck. You do not need the formula underneath; you need to know how to run the test and how to read it.

2. Running the test on two groups

t.test(x, y) takes two numeric vectors from two independent groups. Assign the result to a variable so you can pull out the pieces you need:

salary_hanoi <- c(50, 52, 51, 53, 49, 52)
salary_hcm <- c(53, 55, 54, 52, 56, 54)
res <- t.test(salary_hanoi, salary_hcm)
cat(round(res$p.value, 4), "\n")

Output:

0.0068

Printing res directly shows a long report (t value, degrees of freedom, confidence interval...) - for everyday work you only need two pieces: $p.value and $estimate.

3. Reading the test results

res$estimate gives the mean of each group - exactly the two numbers you will present next to the p-value:

salary_hanoi <- c(50, 52, 51, 53, 49, 52)
salary_hcm <- c(53, 55, 54, 52, 56, 54)
res <- t.test(salary_hanoi, salary_hcm)
print(round(res$estimate, 2))

Output:

mean of x mean of y
    51.17     54.00

mean of x is the mean of the first group, mean of y the second. And res$p.value is the deciding number - remember to round when printing, because the raw p can be very long or switch into scientific notation like 6e-04.

4. The decision threshold and how to conclude

The most common convention is the 0.05 threshold: when p is below 0.05, conclude that the difference is statistically significant. Try it on an A/B experiment where the two variants are nearly even:

conv_a <- c(2.1, 2.3, 2.2, 2.4, 2.2)
conv_b <- c(2.2, 2.3, 2.1, 2.5, 2.3)
res <- t.test(conv_a, conv_b)
cat(round(res$p.value, 4), "\n")

Output:

0.6462

p = 0.6462 is far above 0.05: the small gap between the two variants could easily be due to chance. Written as a decision flow:

conv_a <- c(2.1, 2.3, 2.2, 2.4, 2.2)
conv_b <- c(2.2, 2.3, 2.1, 2.5, 2.3)
p <- t.test(conv_a, conv_b)$p.value
if (p < 0.05) {
  cat("different\n")
} else {
  cat("not enough evidence\n")
}

Output:

not enough evidence

By contrast, with the two offices' salaries in section 2 (p = 0.0068 < 0.05), we conclude the difference is statistically significant.

Key takeaways

  • A small p is evidence of a difference, not a "100% certain" promise - statistics always speaks in probabilities.
  • A large p does NOT prove the two groups are equal - it only means not enough evidence; collecting more data can change the conclusion.
  • 0.05 is a convention, not the truth. Reports should include the p-value itself instead of just saying "yes/no".
  • Compare against the threshold using the raw p; only round when printing to the screen.
  • t.test(x, y) defaults to the two-sample independent test (Welch) - enough for every exercise in this course, no extra arguments needed.

questions.prompt: What range does the value returned by cor(x, y) in R fall into?

options.label: A
options.text: From 0 to 1

options.label: B
options.text: From -1 to 1

options.label: C
options.text: From -100 to 100

options.label: D
options.text: Any real number

questions.explanation: The correlation coefficient always falls between -1 and 1: close to 1 means a strong positive relationship, close to -1 a strong negative relationship, and close to 0 almost no linear relationship.

questions.prompt: An analysis shows cor(overtime, satisfaction) equals -0.92. What is the correct reading?

options.label: A
options.text: Overtime is the direct cause of lower satisfaction

options.label: B
options.text: The two metrics are almost unrelated

options.label: C
options.text: People who work more overtime tend to be less satisfied - a strong negative relationship

options.label: D
options.text: The data must be corrupted because a correlation coefficient cannot be negative

questions.explanation: -0.92 is very close to -1, so this is a strong negative relationship: when one metric is high, the other is low. But correlation does not prove causation - you cannot conclude that overtime CAUSES low satisfaction from this number alone.

questions.prompt: You already have dept_count <- table(dept). Which command produces each department's share of headcount as rounded percentages?

options.label: A
options.text: round(prop.table(dept_count) * 100)

options.label: B
options.text: round(dept_count * 100)

options.label: C
options.text: prop.table(dept)

options.label: D
options.text: table(prop.table(dept_count))

questions.explanation: prop.table() is applied to the RESULT of table() (not directly to the raw vector) and returns proportions that sum to 1. Multiplying by 100 and rounding gives clean percentages for a report.

questions.prompt: A salary test between two offices gives a p-value of 0.03, using the 0.05 threshold. What is the most reasonable conclusion?

options.label: A
options.text: The difference is statistically significant because 0.03 is less than 0.05

options.label: B
options.text: The two offices are 100% guaranteed to have different salary levels

options.label: C
options.text: There is no difference because the p-value is too small

options.label: D
options.text: You must multiply the p-value by 100 before you can compare it

questions.explanation: p = 0.03 < 0.05, so we conclude the difference is statistically significant. But that is probabilistic evidence, not an absolute ironclad guarantee.

questions.prompt: Comparing the conversion of two landing page variants gives a p-value of 0.4. What does that mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The two variants are certainly equally effective

options.label: B
options.text: There is not enough evidence to conclude the two variants differ

options.label: C
options.text: Variant B is better than variant A by exactly 40%

options.label: D
options.text: The test is broken because a p-value must always be below 0.05

questions.explanation: A p above the threshold only says the observed gap could easily be due to chance - meaning NOT ENOUGH evidence, not proof that the two groups are equal. The p-value is also not the percentage difference.

questions.prompt: Which statement is TRUE about a very small p-value, say 0.001?

options.label: A
options.text: It proves with 100% certainty that the two groups differ

options.label: B
options.text: It is strong evidence of a difference, but still a probabilistic conclusion

options.label: C
options.text: It tells you the gap between the two groups is very large

options.label: D
options.text: It tells you the data has too few observations

questions.explanation: A small p means the observed gap is very hard to blame on luck - strong evidence, but never absolute certainty. The p-value also does not measure the SIZE of a difference: a very small gap can still produce a very small p if the sample is large enough.

practice.title: Calling the winner of an A/B test
practice.summaryHtml: The growth team just ran two landing page variants side by side for two weeks. The team lead sends you two series of numbers - the daily metric for variant A and variant B - with a note: "B looks a bit ahead of A, but I got burned once before. This time I want proper statistical backing: is the difference real, or just day-to-day luck?"

sections.title: Requirements
sections.html:
Write a function ab_verdict(group_a, group_b) that takes two numeric vectors - the metric for variant A and variant B. Use the two-group mean-comparison statistical test you have learned to assess the difference, then print exactly 2 lines in the format:

p_value: <p rounded to 4 decimal places>
significant: <yes or no>
  • Line 1: the test's p-value, rounded to 4 decimal places.
  • Line 2: yes if the p-value is below 0.05, otherwise no (compare using the raw, unrounded p-value).
  • Output is plain text: no [1], no quotes.

sections.title: Example 1
sections.html:
Input:

ab_verdict(c(10.2, 9.8, 10.5, 10.1, 9.9, 10.3), c(19.8, 20.4, 20.1, 19.9, 20.6, 20.2))

Output:

p_value: 0
significant: yes

Variant B far outperforms variant A and the data has very little noise - the p-value is so small that rounding to 4 decimal places leaves exactly 0, and the test concludes the difference is statistically significant.

sections.title: Example 2
sections.html:
Input:

ab_verdict(c(2.1, 2.3, 2.2, 2.4, 2.2), c(2.2, 2.3, 2.1, 2.5, 2.3))

Output:

p_value: 0.6462
significant: no

The two variants are nearly identical - the small gap could easily be due to chance, so there is not enough evidence to conclude a difference.
